Are there any triples of consecutive positive integers all of which are powerful (i.e. if $p\mid n$ then $p^2\mid n$)? 
#364: [Er76d][ErGr80,p.68]
number theory | 
powerful
Erdős originally asked Mahler whether there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive powerful numbers, but Mahler immediately observed that the answer is yes from the infinitely many solutions to the Pell equation $x^2=8y^2+1$. 
This conjecture was also made by Mollin and Walsh [MoWa86]. Erdős [Er76d] believed the answer to this question is no, and in fact if $n_k$ is the $k$th powerful number then\[n_{k+2}-n_k > n_k^c\]for some constant $c>0$. The abc conjecture implies there are only finitely many such triples.
It is trivial that there are no quadruples of consecutive powerful numbers since one must be $2\pmod{4}$. 
Chan [Ch25] has shown there are no triples $n-1,n,n+1$ of powerful numbers with $n$ a cube and $n-1,n+1$ both of the shape $p^3x^2$ for some prime $p$ and integer $x$. She [Sh25] has proved there are no triples with $n$ a cube and both $n-1,n+1$ of the shape $p^2x^3$ with $p$ a prime.
By OEIS A076445 there are no such $n$ for $n<7.38\times 10^{28}$.
See also [137], [365], and [938].
Additional thanks to: Alfaiz, Stijn Cambie, Zachary Chase, Yuchen Li, and Desmond Weisenberg

 Regarding the cube case and the general problem: the two remaining mixed shapes, x^3-1=p^2a^3 with x^3+1=q^3z^2, and x^3-1=p^3y^2 with x^3+1=q^2b^3 (p, q prime), are excluded in this preprint (reduction to t^6+t^3+1=3w^2, solved through an elliptic quotient of rank 0).
A further collected volume with three parts is available on Zenodo (concept DOIs, all versions):
- Volume: 10.5281/zenodo.23127546
- Part I, triples (Pell addresses, a height inequality, witnesses): 10.5281/zenodo.23127702
- Part II, pairs and near-consecutive pairs: 10.5281/zenodo.23127704
- Part III, gaps, cyclotomic values, independence tests: 10.5281/zenodo.23127706
Data and scripts: GitHub repository. These are partial results and not a solution of #364. AI assistance is disclosed in the preprints.

A proof 
claimed by Berkay Yüksel Sayim (using Fable 5 by Claude, inside Claude code. doublechecked with chat gpt another model).
 Summary:
 I claim that two mixed forms are impossible for the neighbours of a cube.
Powerful: every prime dividing the number divides it at least twice (72 = 2³·3²). For x ≥ 2 I look at x³−1, x³, x³+1, with primes p, q:
(M1) x³−1 = p²·a³ and x³+1 = q³·z²
(M2) x³−1 = p³·y² and x³+1 = q²·b³
"Mixed": left and right have different shapes. Chan and She excluded equal shapes.
Idea: split x³∓1 = (x∓1)(x²±x+1); look at x mod 3 and where p, q sit: 18 cases. 16 are impossible by known results (e.g. v² = u³+2). In the last case of each form x−1 = t³ and x²−x+1 = 3w², so t⁶+t³+1 = 3w². A rank-0 elliptic curve (SageMath) gives only t = 1, but the cases need t ≥ 7 (M1), t ≤ −5 (M2). So no x works.
Partial result: other shapes are not covered; #364 is not settled.
 Notes:
 Partial result: only these two mixed forms are excluded, other factorizations of the neighbours of a cube are not covered, and #364 is not settled. The key step uses a rank-0 elliptic curve and is computer-assisted (SageMath). I also posted this as a comment in this thread.
